title: GCF and LCM: Two Sides of the Same Factor List
preview: Alternate GCF and LCM through deliberate edges: coprime pairs, multiples of each other, a number with itself, and the GCF(0, n) edge case. Enrichment uses GCF distributively.

body.goal: Students see GCF and LCM as opposite ends of the same factorization — and know when GCF = 1, LCM = product, or both collapse to the number itself.
body.launch: Run the warm-up to refresh the factor-listing move. Then start the slice. Pause after step 3 (coprime case) — it surprises a lot of kids.
body.prerequisiteLabel: Warm up by listing factors and prime factorizations.

prerequisiteSteps.teacherNote: The structural form. Useful for the slice.

steps.teacherNote: Anchor — both have small factor lists. Common factors: 1, 2, 3, 6 → 6.
One is a multiple of the other → GCF is the smaller.
Diamond: coprime numbers. GCF is 1. Many students will hunt and find nothing — let them realize 1 is the answer.
One is a multiple of the other → LCM is the larger.
Diamond: coprime → LCM is the product. Mirror of step 3.
Both have a factor of 2 → LCM ≠ product (which would be 48).
Bigger numbers, multiple shared factors. Use prime factorization if it helps.
Same pair as step 1, but LCM. Look at step 1's answer × this answer = 6 × 36 = 216 = 12 × 18. Coincidence?
Number with itself. GCF and LCM both = 7. Push: 'when does that happen?'
Diamond: zero edge. Every number divides 0, so the GCF is just whatever 6's biggest factor is — itself.

enrichmentSteps.teacherNote: GCF is 6 → factor it out. Distributive property in disguise.
Three numbers — find what divides all three.
Coprime triple → LCM is the product.

body.consolidation: Pull it together. 'Step 1 was GCF(12, 18) = 6. Step 10 was LCM(12, 18) = 36. Multiply them — what do you get? Compare to 12 × 18.' (They equal each other — the GCF × LCM = the product of the original numbers, every time. Not standard 6.NS.6 content, but a nice diamond.) 'On step 11, GCF and LCM came out the same. When does that happen?'
